'''Elmer Lucille Allen''' (born August 23, 1931) is an American [[ceramic art]]ist and [[chemist]]. In 1966, she became the first African-American chemist at [[Brown-Forman]] in [[Louisville, Kentucky]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://nkaa.uky.edu/record.php?note_id=1704|title=Allen, Elmer Lucille · Notable Kentucky African Americans Database|website=nkaa.uky.edu|access-date=February 10, 2016|archive-date=January 26, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170126220212/http://nkaa.uky.edu/record.php?note_id=1704|url-status=dead}}</ref> and worked there for 31 years. In 2004, she became the first recipient of the [[Kentucky Arts Council]] Governor's Award in the Arts for Community Arts.<ref name="Johnson">{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=Marina |title=Louisville celebrates Black History Month with awards ceremony |url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/local/2024/02/05/louisville-ymca-remembers-black-history-month-with-awards-celebration/72453711007/ |date=February 5, 2024 |newspaper=[[Courier Journal]] |access-date=December 14, 2025}}</ref>

== Early life and career ==
Allen was born Elmer Lucille Hammonds on August 23, 1931, to mother Ophelia Guinn Hammonds and father Elmer Hammonds, in Louisville, Kentucky.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Kentucky African American Encyclopedia |date=2015 |publisher=The University Press of Kentucky |page=14 |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/book/40887 |access-date=March 30, 2025 |via=Project Muse |archive-date=January 25, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250125081734/https://muse.jhu.edu/book/40887 |url-status=live }}</ref> Both her father and brother (nicknamed "Bud") were named Elmer and the family chose to name her Elmer Lucille (though at home her family also called her "Cile").<ref name="bourbonwomen">{{Cite web |last=bourbonwomen |date=May 10, 2021 |title=Meet The Makers: Brown-Forman Retired Chemist Elmer Lucille Allen |url=https://bourbonwomen.org/brown-forman-elmer-lucille-allen/ |access-date=November 19, 2025 |website=Bourbon Women Association |archive-date=October 15, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251015122704/https://bourbonwomen.org/brown-forman-elmer-lucille-allen/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Potter |first=Eugenia K. |title=Kentucky Women: Two Centuries of Indomitable Spirit and Vision |publisher=Big Tree Press |year=1997 |isbn=0-9659858-0-6 |page=2}}</ref> She and her family lived in the [[Russell, Louisville|Russell neighborhood]], and she attended Western Elementary.<ref name="90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen">{{Cite web |date=November 8, 2021 |title=90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen |url=https://americanwhiskeymag.com/2021/11/08/elmer-lucille-allen-interview/ |access-date=December 10, 2025 |website=American Whiskey Magazine |archive-date=March 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329201558/https://americanwhiskeymag.com/2021/11/08/elmer-lucille-allen-interview/ |url-status=live }}</ref> At the time, the city was segregated.<ref name="90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen" /> In an interview she stated that she "never went to school with whites" until she was a junior in college.<ref name="Allen">{{Cite web |last=Allen |first=Elmer Lucille |title=Interview with Elmer Lucille Allen, April 4, 2016 |url=https://ohc.library.louisville.edu/ohms/viewer.php?cachefile=2017_074_02_allen.xml |access-date=March 29, 2023 |website=University of Louisville Oral History Center |archive-date=March 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329194208/https://ohc.library.louisville.edu/ohms/viewer.php?cachefile=2017_074_02_allen.xml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen" />

Allen took her first art class, a sewing class, in seventh grade at Madison Street Junior High School. She stated in an interview that the first artist she identified with was her teacher, Ms. Hattie Figg, who taught painting at the junior high. She learned many functional crafts in junior high, such as shoe repair, printing, sewing, and carpentry. She also learned various crafts at the Plymouth Settlement House and Presbyterian Community Center. She was also a Girl Scout, and this activity fostered her interest in art.

Allen graduated from [[Central High School (Louisville, Kentucky)|Central High School]] in 1949, at a time when African-American women had very few opportunities available to them. She attended [[Louisville Municipal College]], a co-ed, all-Black school (part of the [[University of Louisville]]) from 1949 to 1951 and then switched to [[Nazareth College (Kentucky)|Nazareth College]] (now Spalding University) where she was one of only a few Black students.<ref name="90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen" /> She worked as a babysitter and a house cleaner to help pay for college.<ref name="bourbonwomen"/> She graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree from Nazareth College in 1953.<ref name="90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen" />

After graduating from college, Allen had a difficult time finding a chemistry-related job. She moved to Indiana, took the civil service exam and began working as a typist at [[Fort Benjamin Harrison]]. After her time at Fort Benjamin Harrison she worked as a hospital technician at General Hospital, then Methodist Hospital, then Community Hospital in Indianapolis. Allen moved back to Louisville in 1958 and continued to work as a hospital technician, setting up labs at [[Norton Children's Hospital#History|Children's Hospital]].<ref name="artsandsciences.louisville.edu" />

== Chemistry career ==
Allen's first chemistry-related job was at American Synthetic and Rubber Company (ASRC), which shut down shortly after she started. She then moved on to work as a research chemist for Dr. Felix Bronner at the University of Louisville, doing medical and dental research.<ref name="artsandsciences.louisville.edu" />

Through her colleagues and connections she made at UofL, in April 1966, Allen landed a job at Brown-Forman, a [[distillery]] specializing in [[whisky|whiskeys]].<ref name="artsandsciences.louisville.edu" /> When she began working there she was only one of a few woman in a non-secretarial job as well as the first black working for the company.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Glowicki |first=Matthew |title=First Black chemist at Brown-Forman, Elmer Lucille Allen, still creating, learning at 94 |url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/local/2025/09/25/trailblazing-chemist-ceramicist-elmer-lucille-allen-still-creating/85945634007/ |date=September 25, 2025 |access-date=November 19, 2025 |newspaper=[[Courier Journal]]}}</ref> She worked for Brown-Forman for 31 years, rising through the ranks and researching the chemistry involved in the grain-based components of [[Whisky#Production|whiskey making]] (malt, corn, etc.). She retired in 1997.<ref name="90 Years of Elmer Lucille Allen"/>

Allen was honored by the Kentucky Black Bourbon Guild for her significant impact on the [[bourbon whiskey|bourbon]] industry. They recognize her legacy as an inspiration to young black women within the field today. The organization is in the process of developing a commemorative bottle as well as a scholarship fund in her name.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Richardson |first=Rachel |date=February 16, 2024 |title=Black History Month: Chemist Elmer Lucille Allen |url=https://www.lex18.com/community/black-history-month-chemist-elmer-lucille-allen |access-date=November 19, 2025 |website=LEX 18 News – Lexington, KY (WLEX) |archive-date=January 15, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260115051308/https://www.lex18.com/community/black-history-month-chemist-elmer-lucille-allen |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Art career ==
In the 1970s, Allen's doctor recommended she try ceramics as a way to help ease the arthritis in her hands. Through an [[art therapy|art therapist]] at [[Seneca High School MCA|Seneca High School]], she started her ceramic career, in the class she met ceramic graduates from University of Louisville and they suggested that she take classes at the university.<ref name="artsandsciences.louisville.edu">{{Cite web |title=Trailblazer and Community Advocate Elmer Lucille Allen Receives 2025 A&S Alumni Award {{!}} College of Arts & Sciences |url=https://artsandsciences.louisville.edu/news/trailblazer-and-community-advocate-elmer-lucille-allen-receives-2025-alumni-award |access-date=December 4, 2025 |website=artsandsciences.louisville.edu |archive-date=January 20, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260120222247/https://artsandsciences.louisville.edu/news/trailblazer-and-community-advocate-elmer-lucille-allen-receives-2025-alumni-award |url-status=live }}</ref> Starting in 1981 she began to study art at the [[University of Louisville]], receiving her Masters of Creative Arts with a focus in ceramics and fiber in 2002.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.carnegiecenter.org/exhibit_elmerallen.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070812225900/http://www.carnegiecenter.org/exhibit_elmerallen.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 12, 2007 |title=Elmer Lucille Allen: Shibori and Ceramics |website=[[Carnegie Center for Art & History]] |access-date=April 18, 2026}}</ref> Allen's textile work incorporates [[shibori]] dyeing techniques.<ref name=Kramer />

Speaking of her ceramics, Allen states, "I make the things that I want, and I have always liked teapots." She enjoys the fact that if she made something she did not like, she could simply start over again. Her platters are typically dark and molten, while her teapots are colorful and graphic. She states, "When I rented my first studio in 2005 at [[Mellwood Art Center|Mellwood [Art Center]]], I knew that I was truly an artist."<ref>{{cite web |first=Karen R. |last=Davis |url=http://karoda.typepad.com/seamless_skin/2010/11/elmer-lucille-allen-artist-interview.html |title=Elmer Lucille Allen, Artist Interview |website=Seamless Skin |date=November 7, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250911081132/http://karoda.typepad.com/seamless_skin/2010/11/elmer-lucille-allen-artist-interview.html |archive-date=September 11, 2025}}</ref>

In the 1980s, Allen became involved in the Louisville arts scene. She helped form the Kentucky Coalition of African American Arts and was a founding member of the Arts Council of Louisville.<ref name="Allen" />

=== Exhibits ===
* 2010 – "Absence and Presence: The Art of Elmer Lucille Allen and Valerie White" at E&S Gallery, Louisville, Kentucky<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 7, 2010 |title=Elmer Lucille Allen, working in shibori |page=I3 |newspaper=[[The Courier-Journal]]}}</ref> 
* 2011 – ''Powering Creativity: Air, Fuel, Heat'' at the [[Carnegie Center for Art & History]] in [[New Albany, Indiana]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 28, 2011 |title=Powering Creativity: Air, Fuel, Heat |website=[[Carnegie Center for Art & History]] |url=http://carnegiecenter.org/powering-creativity-air-fuel-heat-2/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170213094007/http://carnegiecenter.org/powering-creativity-air-fuel-heat-2/ |archive-date=February 13, 2017 |access-date=February 12, 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2016 – ''Women's Artist Exhibition: The African Heritage Experience'' at the [[Kentucky Center for African American Heritage]] in Louisville<ref>{{cite web |title=2016 Women's Artist Exhibition – KCAAH |url=http://www.kcaah.org/content/2016-women%E2%80%99s-artist-exhibition |website=www.kcaah.org |access-date=February 10, 2016 |archive-date=April 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180410072346/http://www.kcaah.org/content/2016-women%E2%80%99s-artist-exhibition |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2020 – "African-American Women: Celebrating Diversity in Art" at KORE Gallery, Louisville<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 2, 2020 |title=Exhibits |page=4C |newspaper=[[Courier Journal]]}}</ref>
* 2023 – "Remembrance", an exhibition honoring Lida Gordon by Bette Levy, Elmer Lucille Allen, Denise Furnish, and Melinda Snyder at PYRO, Louisville<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 25, 2023 |title=Exhibits |page=2C |newspaper=[[Courier Journal]]}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1969, Allen was very active in her community and created the Chickasaw Little League. The [[Little League Baseball|little league]], in operation 3–4 years, was formed to provide a place for the Black children who lived in the [[Chickasaw, Louisville|Chickasaw neighborhood]] to play baseball. They were discriminated against and were not allowed to participate in the little league held in [[Shawnee Park]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Allen |first=Elmer Lucille |title=Volunteer believes 'one person can make a difference' |url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/opinion/contributors/2015/05/22/volunteer-believes-one-person-can-make-difference/27754019/ |date=May 21, 2015 |access-date=September 29, 2022 |newspaper=[[The Courier-Journal]]}}</ref>

While at Brown-Forman, she met her husband, Roy Allen, who worked in the company's food services.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wheeler |first=Koby |date=October 15, 2024 |title=Elmer Lucille Allen: Chemist, Artist, and Lifelong Learner |url=https://sd2.org/elmer-lucille-allen-chemist-artist-and-lifelong-learner/ |access-date=November 19, 2025 |website=San Diego Squared |archive-date=October 11, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251011005429/https://sd2.org/elmer-lucille-allen-chemist-artist-and-lifelong-learner/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
{{BLP sources section|date=December 2025}}
In 2019, the Imagine 2020 Mural Festival commissioned artist Brandon Marshall to create a mural celebrating the life of Elmer Lucille Allen.<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 13, 2020 |title=Elmer Lucille Allen, barrier-breaking artist, chemist |page=2A |newspaper=[[Courier Journal]]}}</ref>

In August 2025, Allen received an honorary street name sign regarding her contributions to Louisville science and culture, which reads: "Elmer Lucille Allen Way". It is located on the corner of Winnrose Way and Fairland Place in Louisville.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Maloney |first=Renee |date=August 24, 2025 |title=93-year-old Louisville woman receives honorary street name sign |url=https://www.wlky.com/article/louisville-woman-receives-honorary-street-name/65878462 |access-date=November 19, 2025 |work=[[WLKY]] |archive-date=September 8, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250908193837/https://www.wlky.com/article/louisville-woman-receives-honorary-street-name/65878462 |url-status=live }}</ref>

She has also received the following awards:
* 2004 – Governor's Award in the Arts (Kentucky), Community Arts; first-ever recipient<ref name="Johnson" />
* 2004 – Woman of Distinction 
* 2007 – "Women of Spunk" from [[Actors Theatre of Louisville|Actors Theatre]]
* 2011 – Caritas Medal from [[Spalding University]];<ref>{{Cite magazine |url=http://louisville.epubxp.com/i/43017-fall-2011/51 |title=Class Notes |magazine=University of Louisville Magazine |page=50 |date=Fall 2011 |publisher=louisville.epubxp.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170213164009/http://louisville.epubxp.com/i/43017-fall-2011/51 |archive-date=February 13, 2017 |access-date=February 12, 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref> highest award given by Spalding to alumni
* 2015 – [[KMAC Museum|Kentucky Museum of Art and Craft]]'s Art Advocacy Award<ref name=Kramer>{{Cite news |first=Elizabeth |last=Kramer |url=http://www.courier-journal.com/story/entertainment/arts/visual/2015/10/22/elmer-allens-giving-spirit-garners-prize/73540328/ |title=Elmer Allen's giving spirit garners prize |date=October 22, 2015 |newspaper=[[The Courier-Journal]] |access-date=February 12, 2017}}</ref>
* 2015 – Community Spirit Award given by the [[University of Louisville]] College of Arts and Science and the Yearlings Club
* 2016 – Parkland Rising Up Project
* 2016 – ''[[Louisville Defender]]'' – Lifetime Community Service Recognition Award
* 2016 – Outstanding Community Leader by Metro Council
* 2019 – [[Louisville Free Public Library]]'s Pillars of Louisville<ref>{{Cite web|last=Jones|first=Michael L.|date=February 1, 2019|title=Artist and activist Elmer Lucille Allen honored as one of the Pillars of Louisville|url=https://louisvilleinsight.com/archived-news/artist-and-activist-elmer-lucille-allen-honored-as-one-of-the-pillars-of-louisville/|website=Louisville Insight}}</ref>
